sections.heading: Abstract
sections.where: Title page, Solana Constellation, Internet Capital Markets, Quentin Kniep, Max Resnick, Jakub Sliwinski, Roger Wattenhofer, Anza, White Paper v0.9, March 25, 2026
paragraphs: A chain that is supposed to host worldwide financial markets has to be built so that participants cannot push it around. Safety and liveness keep the system working, and they have been the main research target. Consensus has made blockchains much faster, but a different weakness is still common: privileged parties can change how long a transaction waits and where it is placed, and they can use that power against users. Constellation is Solana's multiple-concurrent-proposer protocol. On top of the usual guarantees it adds selective censorship resistance, justified by incentives. The intended effect is that latency and order stay fair, and that users are not exposed to that kind of abuse. The paper claims that among production blockchain protocols, Constellation has the fastest economic tick that the protocol itself enforces and that resists censorship, and it gives 50 ms as that tick.

Attesters form an extra layer of nodes. They depend on synchronized clocks so that transactions are handled on time and cannot be quietly dropped. The economic ticks, meaning the intervals in which transactions are included, are not forced to wait out a full global network delay.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.where: Page 1, heading only; body is in 1.1 and 1.2
paragraphs: The introduction is a heading over two subsections. The first treats a rotating leader's brief monopoly on inclusion and order as extractable profit once a chain is busy, and treats designs that merely share that profit as still harmful to users. The second outlines concurrent proposers and attesters that leave a leader in place but force that leader to assemble blocks from inputs it does not freely choose.

sections.heading: 1.1 Motivation
paragraphs: Blockchain protocols are meant to take transaction platforms out of any single actor's control and in a wider sense, to democratize them. In practice many designs still give some participant a temporary monopoly on which transactions enter a block and in what order. Under a leader schedule, the leader of the moment sees every pending transaction, may reorder them, may drop any it dislikes, and may insert its own transactions so as to front-run users or disrupt them in other ways. The paper treats exploitation of that monopoly as damage to the product and to the market. The same structure exists on every blockchain platform, but it only becomes visible once there is enough economic activity. Once a chain is mature enough to be studied, validators increasingly leave the prescribed behavior and profit at users' expense. Nodes that keep following the rules then earn less, so they too are pushed to undermine the system they run.

Profit taken from the leader's monopoly is called maximal extractable value, with Daian and coauthors cited. Early responses mostly fell back on centralized services that users had to trust, because those services gave application developers a smoother product, while decentralized and trustless answers stayed out of reach. Proposer-builder separation, with Buterin cited, is presented as a prominent design that accepts this value and tries to maximize it. Specialized builders compete to construct the block that extracts the most, and the proposer picks the most profitable block.

Less sophisticated operators can then share revenue from the temporary monopoly, which narrows differences in who can reach those opportunities. The paper's judgment is that this eases some of the damage MEV can do to the nodes, and does nothing to reduce the damage to users. Extraction is optimized and redistributed, and the users' loss is maximized. Constellation is set in the opposite direction: remove the incentive to exploit the monopoly, so that users are treated fairly.

Traditional markets try to limit analogous abuse with jurisdictional rules and regulatory oversight. Those mechanisms supply some accountability, yet they react after the fact and differ from place to place. The paper points to repeated high-profile failures in centralized exchanges and markets as evidence that regulatory safeguards have limits. The aim here is to prevent the abuse in the design itself. Multiple concurrent proposers are used to end dominance by a single leader. A formal leader role remains, but that leader is tightly constrained and must assemble blocks from the inputs supplied by proposers and attesters. The claimed result is a standardized, enforceable market structure that advances Solana toward a universal venue for economic activity.

sections.heading: 1.2 Protocol Overview
paragraphs: Users may address a transaction to a single proposer or to more than one. Each cycle, every proposer chooses which transactions to bundle and ships them to the attesters as erasure-coded pslices, broken into pshreds. The leading p is only a written mark so these objects stay distinct from Alpenglow slices and shreds, and it is not pronounced. An attester stamps the time, then passes every pshred it holds to the leader along with an attestation, which is how the leader is forced to keep data that is both correct and required. The leader, once per cycle, assembles the transactions that gathered enough attestations into a batch. That batch is the Constellation counterpart of an Alpenglow slot's block. Rotor, Alpenglow's dissemination protocol, carries the batch to every validator. Several cycles of batches are the payload inside the leader's block. Validators check the block and cast votes with Votor.

Figure 1 draws that lifecycle in five stages: a user submits a transaction, a proposer sends pslices, an attester forwards and attests them, the leader proposes a batch, and relays disseminate it. Columns run user, proposer, attester, leader, relay, validator, and the drawing tags the right-hand side Alpenglow. Gray arrows are extra copies kept so the path survives loss. The caption's claim is that the receiver can continue once half the arriving packets are in hand.

sections.heading: 2 Model
paragraphs: The model section says that apart from small departures, Constellation stays close to Alpenglow's model. The departures are developed in the two subsections that follow: assumptions about faults, time, clocks, stake, and an economic fairness property, and the cryptographic tools used to encode proposals and to check them.

sections.heading: 2.1 Protocol Assumptions
paragraphs: Some nodes may be Byzantine and may misbehave in arbitrary ways. They can omit a send, and they can collude. Signing inconsistent information is given as a fault that can be proved. A late send cannot be punished, because the cause might be an extreme network delay rather than malice. The stake bounds are imported unchanged from Alpenglow. Taken together, Byzantine nodes are assumed to hold strictly less than 20 percent of stake. A further slice, as large as 20 percent, may have crashed. Every node outside those two groups is correct and obeys the rules.

The network model is partial synchrony with a global stabilization time, citing Constantinescu and coauthors together with Dwork, Lynch, and Stockmeyer. A message between correct nodes does arrive eventually, yet the wait can be unbounded. Safety does not depend on speed. Under arbitrary delay, the asynchronous case, every correct node emits the same blocks in the same sequence. Liveness holds only in synchronous periods, when delivery is quick, so correct nodes keep emitting transactions while messages among them arrive promptly. Synchrony, in this model, means one global worst-case delivery bound, written delta. Before the unknown GST, delay is unlimited. Afterward, a message m sent at t_m is in hand by the later of GST and t_m, plus that bound.

During synchrony the protocol will rarely wait out a timeout. The actual delay between correct nodes is written as a smaller delta. The paper claims that in practice this actual delay is often far below the worst-case bound. The real delay varies and is unknown. It is not part of the protocol and is used only in the latency analysis. For protocols that answer as soon as messages arrive, ordinary-case latency tracks the actual delay alone, and ignores the worst-case bound.

Alpenglow can run with a purely logical clock. Constellation instead needs a wall clock that stays close to UTC. The paper treats putting time into a distributed protocol as an established technique and cites Google Spanner. It says reasonably accurate time can be obtained in several ways, including a GPS receiver or the chrony daemon, which it describes as an improvement on legacy ntpd. Data centers are said to often have an excellent time source, with Google TrueTime and Amazon's time sync service named, and financial centers are said to as well.

The population is n nodes, as in Alpenglow. In that earlier design a node is always a validator, sometimes a relay, and only rarely a leader. Constellation adds proposer and attester as further occasional jobs on those same machines. Node v_i is drawn for the extra jobs at random in proportion to a positive stake rho_i. Communication uses authenticated messages. Some of Constellation's messages are too large for one UDP datagram, which Alpenglow did not require. Attestations on the path from attester to leader are the example.

Most of the correctness argument is inherited from Alpenglow. A blockchain's job is one sequence of finalized blocks so that every node applies transactions in one shared order. Each block points at a parent, starting from a notional genesis block. Finalized blocks make a single parent-to-child chain, and finalizing one block finalizes every ancestor. Slot numbers are natural numbers and set the order, with a child slot above its parent's slot. Each slot either finalizes a block that the leader produced or else produces a skip. Those finalized slots are delivered to execution in slot order.

The safety claim: once a correct node has finalized block b in slot s, any later-or-equal slot s-prime in which any correct node finalizes a block b-prime must have b-prime descending from b. The liveness claim: whenever synchrony lasts long enough, correct nodes finalize fresh blocks that correct nodes produced.

Beyond safety and liveness, the paper adds an economic fairness property it names selective censorship resistance. Suppose a correct proposer hands in transaction tx during cycle c. Then some cycle c-prime, no later than c plus lambda, carries tx in its batch, or else the chain has no batch in any cycle from that c-prime through c plus lambda. A fee-competitive tx is executed. Strong fee-competitiveness, inside a proposed set T that already contains tx, means tx sits in the highest-bid subset whose compute units add up to at most bcu. Weak fee-competitiveness means Algorithm 6 places tx in the scheduled set. The paper says the selection rule is arranged so that strong fee-competitiveness in T implies weak fee-competitiveness in T.

sections.heading: 2.2 Cryptographic Techniques
paragraphs: The hash function is collision-resistant, and SHA-256 is given as an example. Digital signatures are secure and unforgeable, and each node knows every other node's public key. For integers Gamma at least gamma, both at least 1, a (Gamma, gamma) erasure code turns a bit string M whose length is m into Gamma pieces, each of size m divided by gamma plus a term on the order of log Gamma. The extra term indexes the piece. Any gamma pieces can efficiently reconstruct M. Reconstruction also receives the length m, which is assumed constant, with shorter payloads padded. In this protocol a pslice payload is encoded with a (Gamma_p, gamma_p) Reed-Solomon code, citing Reed and Solomon. Any gamma_p of the pieces rebuild M. The data expansion rate is Gamma_p divided by gamma_p.

A Merkle tree, citing Merkle, commits to an ordered vector of pieces under a collision-resistant hash. It is a full binary tree. Leaves are piece hashes, each joined with a marker that says the hash is a leaf. Every internal node hashes its two children, and the root is the commitment. A position's validation path is the sibling of each node from that leaf up to the root. Showing the root and the path shows that the piece sits at that index. The check rebuilds the path hashes and accepts the proof only when the rebuilt root matches the commitment. On success, that piece is the data at the claimed index for that root. Because the hash resists collisions, a different piece cannot carry a valid proof for the same index.

Encoding, citing Cachin and Tessaro, takes a payload M of size m, erasure-codes it, builds a Merkle tree on the piece hashes, and returns the root together with each piece and its path. The root is uniquely associated with M. Decoding takes the root and a set of gamma indexed pieces, each of the right length and each valid for that root at its position. The routine must also make sure that the root is correctly computed from all Gamma pieces of some message, or it fails. Failure guarantees that no set of gamma pieces tied to that root can be decoded, and that the root was provably constructed maliciously. To get that pass-or-fail behavior, decode rebuilds a candidate message from the given pieces, re-encodes it into a full vector, builds a new Merkle tree, and returns the candidate only when the new root equals the given root. Otherwise it fails.

sections.heading: 3 Constellation Protocol
paragraphs: This section specifies the Constellation protocol in detail. It opens by sketching the roles that carry a transaction from the user through proposal, attestation, and block assembly, and then gives the definitions and the pseudocode for the objects those roles create, forward, attest, and check.

sections.heading: 3.1 Roles
paragraphs: A user may give a signed transaction to one proposer or to several. A bitmap of p bits names the allowed proposers, and any proposer missing from that bitmap is forbidden to include the transaction. Required fields are a compute ceiling tx.cu, a priority fee tx.bid, and a nonce that limits the transaction to one execution. An inclusion fee is also due, computed from the byte length and from the signature count. The fuller transaction rules are postponed to Section 3.3.

About 16 proposers are assigned for each cycle. The set changes over time: once per leader window, the oldest proposer is replaced by a new one drawn at random by stake. A proposer may accept or reject transactions freely, as long as every accepted transaction is valid. At most about four times per cycle, and possibly less often, the proposer ships one bundle of transactions, a pslice, to the attesters. The pslice is shredded across all q attesters with fourfold redundancy, so a quarter of the pshreds are enough to reconstruct it.

Attesters are assigned from the same wall-clock schedule. About 256 attesters are concurrent in each cycle, chosen at random by stake and replaced in the same manner as proposers. They receive pshreds and forward them to the leader immediately. At the end of the cycle they build an attestation over the last delta-worth of pslices they saw, which the paper identifies with the last mu times lambda pslice indices, and they send that attestation to the leader. To handle leader handover and faulty leaders, attestations and the corresponding data should go not only to the current leader but to about two next leaders in total.

As a side remark, cycles named inside attestations can serve as an on-chain clock. Seeing those cycles is taken as proof that the middle attester, ordered by wall clock, is already past that instant. The clock may be exposed per batch or per block, since cycle indices must rise strictly from one point on the chain to the next. Figure 2 draws two attesters across two cycles, each signing a different subset of the numbered pslices that two proposers sent.

A single leader assembles the block. It holds back until attestations, plus the accompanying pshreds, have arrived from q/2 attesters. Those attestations are written into the block. A pslice named by at least q/4 attestations can be rebuilt from its pshreds, and the leader is obliged to include every pslice that meets that same count. Where a proposer misbehaved, the leader appends a fraud witness after the other block contents. An attestation that does not check is discarded.

When many attesters name the same proposal, the leader stores the pslice reference a single time and per attester, keeps a signature plus an index into that list. Every distinct proposal contributes its proposer commitment. Every proposal that is valid and included also contributes its transaction bytes in full. Attestations and decoded batches leave the leader one batch at a time through Rotor. The coding on that path is the twofold erasure code the paper attributes to standard Alpenglow.

Validators, about 1,000 of them, execute in a pipeline while batches are still arriving. After the leader's whole block is present they repeat Alpenglow's usual validity checks, and they also demand that the batches inside the leader's shreds be the batches the attestations name. All of those checks must succeed or the block is not valid. Voting in the failure case is unchanged from Alpenglow. What follows turns the role sketch into definitions. Familiarity with Alpenglow is assumed: slots, nodes, and much else are inherited, and some of those definitions are altered or extended.

sections.heading: 3.2 Role Schedule
paragraphs: An epoch is still Alpenglow's logical-time epoch, a fixed run of slots. Who participates in epoch e plus one, and with what stake, is fixed when epoch e minus one ends. Near the close of epoch e, proposers and attesters can briefly be unsure whether epoch e plus one has begun. For that short overlap Constellation runs both epochs at once, with two proposer sets and two attester sets live together. Which cycles fall in which epoch is Alpenglow's decision. Cycles themselves come from UTC. Wall time is cut into steps of about 50 ms, and the cycle counter advances once per step. The index is the 64-bit nanosecond Unix timestamp divided by 50,000,000, and a new cycle begins on an exact multiple. Those cycles do not line up with Alpenglow slots.

Figure 3 sets the attester clock against the consensus clock. The attester row, spelled attestors on the figure, is a fixed grid of real-time periods, each one cycle long. Consensus moves when ParentReady fires, not on that grid. The drawing annotates the cycle length, the block length, and a timeout, and it numbers leader blocks and validator blocks under the words cycle, block, and ParentReady.

Definition 1, given the validator set and stake of epoch e and slot s, reuses Alpenglow's leader as leader of epoch and slot. It adds proposer of epoch and cycle at index j, returning that proposer or bottom, for j from 1 through p, and attester of epoch and cycle at index k, for k from 1 through q. Both sets change slowly. The oldest proposer or attester is replaced every tau cycles, with tau about 32, once per leader window. The paper writes that window as w times the block duration divided by the cycle length. Proposer index j is replaced in cycle c when c minus j times tau is congruent to 0 modulo p times tau. For attesters the test is c minus k times tau congruent to 0 modulo q times tau.

If the node at proposer index j changes between cycle c and the next cycle, the next lambda cycles at that index are bottom, an empty assignment, and the successor node starts only after the gap. The paper treats the hole as a separation of one delivery bound between successive holders of the same index. The hole also cuts the effective proposer count by one. Later rules get simpler because of it. Each list in Definition 5 can be read as commitments from a single node. When a misbehaving proposer's payload is dropped, no adjacent holder of that same index is dropped along with it.

sections.heading: 3.3 Transactions
paragraphs: Alpenglow can ignore what a transaction contains. Constellation cannot. A meter prices execution in compute units, and every transaction declares a ceiling cu. Cost is forbidden to rise past cu. The instant it does, execution is canceled and the fee is still due. A separate bid is the per-unit execution price, and that bid is what ranks transactions that share a batch. The charge is cu multiplied by the bid even when execution does not finish, and even when the transaction burns fewer units than it reserved.

Handing the same transaction to k proposers multiplies the inclusion fee by k. The priority charge, cu times the bid, is taken only once, because execution itself happens once. The paper expects those priority fees to dominate what users pay, and says the proceeds return to the ecosystem in proportion to stake.

The fee payer account must hold enough to cover the cost, or proposers will not include the transaction. The paper calls this check intricate and postpones it to Section 3.7. A nonce, described as a bankhash system, ensures the transaction is executed only once even if several proposers include it. Transactions run in batches, and Section 3.8 describes which transactions a batch contains. At a high level a transaction must pass several tests. A proposer must include it. It must collect enough attestations for the leader to put it in the batch. Its bid must be high enough for it to be executed. Finally the whole block must be confirmed by Alpenglow. The third step is described as non-trivial, and the paper says it is likely that not every transaction that gets on chain can also be executed.

A transaction that is not time critical may include an optional tag tx.expire and be handled in a best-effort way. The protocol admits it at the first cycle where its bid wins a place against the other transactions competing that cycle, and it may keep being considered until cycle tx.expire. After that cycle the transaction is discarded and not executed. Time-critical transactions can omit the tag. They want to be considered only in the first cycle in which they become valid, which the paper defines as the first cycle that has enough attestations.

sections.heading: 3.4 Proposers
paragraphs: Proposers named by the schedule collect transactions and send them as a pslice that has been erasure-coded into pshreds. Definition 2 is the hash commitment of a transaction list: hash the concatenation of the individual transaction hashes, in order. A proposer is limited in how much data it may submit per cycle, and it submits that data in at most mu different chunks, the pslices. Each pslice is erasure-coded into Gamma_p pshreds. Later, that commitment hash is how others check the leader's included transactions against what attesters signed. The pslice's Merkle root has a different role. It lets a leader detect a misbehaving proposer and include a proof, under Definition 7, that the pslice was built incorrectly, for example because decode fails. If the proposer behaved correctly, that root is not mentioned in disseminated blocks. In the paper's terms, the commitment hash binds the leader, and the Merkle root shields the leader.

Definition 3 gives a pshred as epoch, cycle, proposer index, pslice index, shred index, commitment hash, Merkle root, the data piece and its Merkle path, and a signature. The shred index runs from 1 through Gamma_p. The signature is the proposer's signature on the pslice object of that epoch, cycle, proposer index, pslice index, hash, and root. The pslice index is tied to the cycle: it must be greater than (c minus 1) times mu and at most c times mu. The paper says the cycle field could be omitted because of that inequality and is kept only for clarity. The main purpose of the inequality is to bound later overhead, so that even in the worst case the chain cannot contain too many hashes that refer to different pslice indexes.

Definition 4 says a pslice is any set of those pshreds whose index set has size gamma_p, and it sets Gamma_p equal to q, the number of attesters. Decoding the root and the pieces must return a transaction list, so the same pslice is also the tuple of epoch, cycle, proposer index, pslice index, hash, root, the transaction list, and the signature. The helper that builds shreds, called by the scheduled proposer, returns one shred per index. The cycle stamped on a pslice records when the proposer built it, rather than a forecast of when later stages should handle it.

Algorithm 1 runs for a node when the clock equals c times the cycle length and that node is proposer index j in the epoch. It sets a base index to (c minus 1) times mu, then loops i from 1 through mu. A proposer-specific function selects the transactions. An empty list produces no pslice. Otherwise the pslice index is the base plus i, the list is hashed under Definition 2, shreds are built, and shred k is sent to attester k. The proposer then waits until the clock equals c times the cycle length plus i times the cycle length divided by mu. Intuitively the chosen transactions are the highest-value valid ones the proposer has for the pslice it is about to send. How a proposer ranks them is allowed to vary, and the paper places that policy outside this work.

sections.heading: 3.5 Attesters
paragraphs: An attester collects pshreds and signs lists of the commitment hashes those pshreds advertised. It ships each pshred onward to the leader at once, and it emits its attestation when the cycle closes. Definition 5's cycle is the attestation's own cycle, often different from the cycle the proposers wrote. The lists cover pslices from the preceding span of length delta, which absorbs the trip from proposer to attester. The object is an epoch, a cycle, an attester index, p lists, and a signature. No list is longer than mu times lambda, and each entry is a proposer cycle, a pslice index, and a hash. What gets signed is not the raw lists but an object whose fields are hashes of each list's concatenated entries.

Figure 4 draws those p lists across a window of mu times lambda pslice indices, running from just after (c minus lambda) times mu through c times mu, with the signature under the hashed lists. If a hash appears in the list for proposer index j, the attestation attests that proposer's pslice at the recorded index and commitment, abbreviated as the tuple of epoch, proposer cycle, index, pslice index, and hash. Every listed pslice index must be greater than (c minus lambda) times mu and at most c times mu. The paper reads that inequality as accepting every proposer message that took no longer than delta to reach the attesters. After the global stabilization time, if the network behaves normally, every correct proposal is attested. The inequality assumes synchronized clocks between proposers and attesters.

To also tolerate a clock skew, the paper widens the window. The lower end subtracts the ceiling of (delta plus the skew) divided by the cycle length, and the upper end adds the ceiling of the skew divided by the cycle length, with both ends then multiplied by mu.

Algorithm 2 keeps a buffer of length mu times lambda for each proposer, initially empty. The forward loop walks an attester window of p times tau cycles from the window's start. While the clock is before the next cycle boundary, a pshred arrives from a proposer. Its pslice index maps to a buffer slot, or to no slot if the index is above c times mu or no greater than (c minus lambda) times mu, which the comments call future or too old. A usable slot index is the pslice index minus (c minus lambda) times mu. The printed condition then stores the pslice index and hash only when that slot is already occupied, and forwards the pshred to each of the next kappa leaders.

At the cycle boundary an attestation is built from the buffered pairs, one list per proposer, and sent to those same next leaders, reliably, by retransmission or by erasure coding. A shift then drops a prefix of each buffer and pads with empty slots. The stored pairs in this listing are index and hash, whereas Definition 5's triples also include a proposer cycle. The shift's comment says it removes the oldest cycle, while the assignment drops a prefix whose length is written as lambda and restores the buffer to length mu times lambda.

sections.heading: 3.6 Leader
paragraphs: Block contents are what the leader builds out of attestations. Attesters run Alpenglow along with everyone else, so a ParentReady event tells them who leads next. Both the pshreds they hold and the attestations they sign go to the upcoming kappa leaders, not merely to the leader of the moment. A faulty current leader would otherwise leave its successor with an empty window and nothing valid to put in blocks. The leader still writes the blocks, but it cannot drop a pslice once enough attesters have recorded that pslice's commitment hash. A block that omits such a pslice is not valid.

Definition 6 makes a submission an ordered transaction list, hashed as a whole. Each submission lines up with one pslice. Outside a stretch in which the chain simply has no batches, a correctly disseminated pslice becomes one submission inside a block. Correct proposers are promised inclusion. A bad proposer still has to be prevented from jamming everyone else. Definition 7 is that proposer's fault witness for a given epoch and cycle: a set of pshreds sharing epoch, cycle, proposer index, and pslice index, plus at least one of two defects. Two of the shreds may disagree on the commitment hash or on the pslice root. Or gamma_p distinct shreds may be present while decode fails or yields a pslice that is not valid. With that witness, the leader keeps the proposer's bytes out of the payload.

Definition 9 is the next container: submissions plus enough attestation material to show that no correct proposer was left out. Definition 8 first allows a shorter encoding. In the list that stands in for the original p lists, each slot is either the list itself or only the hash of that list, and the tuple is still treated as an attestation. Its omitted set gathers every scheduled proposer, on cycles after c minus lambda and up through c, whose slot was swapped for a hash. A slot that remains a list still attests any pslice whose hash appears in it. Because Definition 1 inserts empty cycles when a proposer index changes, the indexes inside one list all belong to one proposer, so omitting that list drops at most that one proposer, or the empty schedule value. A misbehaving proposer can therefore be hashed out without taking a neighbor with them.

A batch is epoch, cycle, a set of exactly alpha attester indices for that cycle, an attestation for every one of those indices, and a list of submissions. Its cycle number is the cycle in which those attestations were made. The pslices they name can come from any moment in the delta leading up to the end of that cycle. If at least gamma_p attestations attest one tuple of epoch, proposer cycle, proposer index, pslice index, and hash, that tuple is attested in the batch. The paper uses the same name for the set of all such tuples. The omitted set of the batch is the proposers whose list was replaced by a hash in any of its attestations. The displayed formula writes that set as a quantification over the attestations; the union symbol in front of the quantifier is not printed.

Hashes belonging to misbehaving proposers can be left out of the attestations in a batch. Which attestation includes which hash can then be encoded as a bitmap of p times mu times lambda bits per attester, and the paper states that alpha times that many bits equals 6 KiB. Assuming the choices in Table 1, it states that the attestation data in every batch would be roughly p times mu times lambda times (32 bytes plus 8 bytes), plus alpha times (64 bytes plus 1 byte), plus 6 KiB, which it gives as about 29.1 KiB. The groups in that sum are labeled as the hash count, the hash, the indexes, the signature, an index, and the bitmap. The brace marks above the formula are broken on the page, while the arithmetic line is intact.

The calculation uses the pslice-index inequality to assume at most mu times lambda commitment hashes per correct proposer in a batch, and it assumes the leader omits the hashes of incorrect proposers. Putting all of the relevant attestation data in every batch is described as a simplification. Consecutive attestations largely overlap, because each covers a full delta of proposer hashes, so new batches can omit repeated content and the attestation bytes can shrink further.

Definition 10 widens an Alpenglow block. The payload now holds the batches plus a byte string the paper calls the garbage pile. highestCycle reads the cycle of the final batch. Batches are the part that matters. The pile exists so validators can confirm the leader stayed honest, and it can be thrown away soon afterward. Fault witnesses are one thing the leader puts there. Validators apply them when they test Definition 12, then vote inside Alpenglow if the block is good. A later repair, which Alpenglow already allows, may ask another node for the block. At that point some correct node has already cleared the leader, so the paper says the pile itself is never part of repair. The specification keeps attestations inside batches, while noting they could live on the pile instead, be deleted as soon as they have been checked, and be left out of repair.

Definition 11 supplies notation for validity and for the pseudocode. For a block with a parent and a sequence of batches, the attested set of the block is every tuple attested in the batches of all ancestors: the parent's attested set, united with the attested set of each of this block's batches. The newly attested list of one batch is the lexicographically sorted list of tuples that this batch attests and that are not already in the parent's attested set or in any earlier batch of the same block.

Algorithm 3 builds a block from the parent. The leader chooses a start cycle strictly above the parent's highest cycle, and that choice is marked as leader-specific. It copies the parent's attested set and starts an empty garbage pile. For each successive cycle it waits for alpha attestations together with their data, builds a batch, and broadcasts the batch on Rotor with the last-slice flag false. Fault witnesses are added to the pile. If the time remaining is less than a batch duration, the loop stops. Otherwise the attested set absorbs the new batch. At the end, the garbage pile is broadcast on Rotor with the last-slice flag true.

Building a batch walks tuples attested by the new attestations but not previously attested. Matching pshreds are collected by epoch, cycle, proposer, pslice index, and hash, and a decode is attempted. If the pslice is invalid for any reason, the shred set is kept as a fault witness. Otherwise the pslice is kept, and one submission is created per pslice, carrying epoch, cycle, proposer index, pslice index, and the transactions.

Under Definition 12 a block is valid only if every batch satisfies three tests. The newly attested tuples and the submissions are the same length, and the hash of the submission in each position equals the hash inside the tuple in that position. Every proposer the batch marks omitted has a fault witness on the garbage pile, for an epoch, cycle, and index that the schedule assigns to that proposer. The earliest batch sits on a cycle above the parent's highest cycle, and each later batch advances the cycle by exactly one. Read as consequences: the leader must supply a submission for every newly attested pslice and for no others; omitted attestation data must be backed by a witness; cycle numbers move in steps of one inside the block and never go backward.

Algorithm 4 is the validator. Executing a batch unions the transactions across its submissions, runs the selection routine, and asks the virtual machine to execute that set in parallel. At the end of the block, a passing validity check waits until the last batch has executed and then emits a Block event that triggers Alpenglow voting. A failing check calls Alpenglow's path that tries to skip the window.

Algorithm 5 checks attestations against the garbage pile. It accumulates tuples attested by each batch and not attested earlier. For every fault witness it looks for newly attested tuples with the same epoch, cycle, and proposer index. If there are none, the block is rejected. Otherwise those hashes are removed from the set that still must appear as submissions. A batch whose cycle is not strictly above the running maximum is rejected. A further test, whose comment says it catches a cycle that is not consecutive inside the block, fires only when the running maximum is already greater than the block's highest cycle and the batch's cycle exceeds the running maximum by more than one. Each submission hash must sit in the remaining set and is then consumed. If any attested hash is left, the block is rejected.

sections.heading: 3.7 Fee Payer Check
paragraphs: Collecting fees is harder once many proposers work at once. Two transactions that debit the same fee payer can be aimed at different proposers, and one transaction can drain an account another transaction is counting on for its fee. A proposer must decide, from local information alone, that the fee can be covered, because it cannot watch the other proposers' intake. Left unsolved, the paper warns, a malicious user could lure proposers into accepting transactions that pay nothing, shove honest transactions out of the payload, and slow the system without spending anything. The warning's last clause is printed as not address, which reads as a missing ending on the word addressed.

The fix is a reserve: a small balance every fee payer must retain. The stated floor is about 0.001 SOL, and it is what keeps the inclusion fee payable. The charging rules are woven into Algorithm 6 so each abuse case is handled. A transaction is left off the execution schedule when taking its priority fee, cu times the bid, would eat into the reserve. If the execution itself would break the reserve, the transaction fails. Upsilon is how many cycles, in the ordinary case after GST, can elapse from the moment one proposer emits a pslice until another proposer sees that pslice's contents inside a finalized block. Adding lambda, the paper says bounds that ordinary interval of doubt about how many transactions have already been accepted.

A user raises the reserve by paying funds in through a transaction. Closing the account removes the reserve entirely, and a special transaction can lower it as far as the minimum phi. Either of those reductions waits upsilon plus lambda cycles before it takes effect, long enough that inclusion fees still owed can be collected before proposers see the account close. The sketch then changes several stages. A proposer skips a transaction once it sees the fee payer's reserve already broken, by a close or by fees already taken. It also skips any transaction in a pslice of cycle c until it has seen a finalized block at cycle c minus upsilon or later. Across any window of upsilon plus lambda cycles, and for one fee payer, the inclusion fees a proposer accepts add up to at most the reserve divided by p.

Leaders and validators count, per fee payer, how many transactions each proposer put in. Crossing the rate from the previous rule makes that pslice invalid. An honest leader then emits no submission for it, and validators reject a block that carries such a submission anyway. Payload handling changes as well. While Algorithm 6 is choosing transactions, the inclusion fee is taken even when the balance falls under the reserve. If the priority fee would push the same account under the reserve, the transaction stays off the schedule. When the priority fee does fit, it is taken before the transaction runs. Should the run itself leave the balance short of the reserve, the transaction fails.

sections.heading: 3.8 Transaction Selection
paragraphs: Leader and validators have to settle on the same set of transactions for a batch. The simple picture is to admit as many as the priority of Definition 13 allows. Parallel execution makes the real rule tighter. A transaction is identified with a four-field tuple: an inclusion field, an ordering field, a compute-unit ceiling, and a hash. The sentence next to the tuple speaks of bid, compute limit, and hash, so the ordering field is the bid, and the three printed tests never look at the inclusion field. Under the printed relation, t is at most t-prime when t's bid is higher, or the bids match and t's compute ceiling is smaller, or those match too and t's hash is smaller or equal. SortTxs sorts ascending under that relation, so the favored transactions come out first.

About four lanes run in parallel. A transaction brings an estimated duration, its compute ceiling, and the writable accounts it might touch. Walk the priority order. Place the transaction at the earliest moment on any lane where it does not overlap a higher-priority transaction that shares an account, and where it still ends by the batch budget: start plus its compute ceiling is at most bcu. That bcu figure is described as the sequential budget of one lane. Ties among free lanes go to the lowest lane index. Gaps are allowed. A later transaction may sit in a gap unless some conflicting higher-priority transaction starts even later. The walk ends when nothing else fits.

Figure 5 shows one run of that packing. Transactions are labeled t1 through t13 in Definition 13 order, each tagged with the accounts it writes, across m lanes, on an axis from zero compute units to bcu. The caption accounts for a gap in front of t8: t8 must wait on t3, it outranks other transactions that could have started right after t5, and the hole is too short for any later transaction. A further transaction, t12 on accounts A and D, has the same compute ceiling as t13 and still cannot be placed, because it must wait on t9 and both of them write account D.

Algorithm 6 is declared not optimal. Take transactions that never share an account, so they are fully independent, and suppose their compute ceilings sum to m times bcu. The paper says it is NP-complete to decide whether some legal schedule contains every one of them. The sum's glyph is damaged: a stray mark sits over a repeated compute-ceiling term, and reading it as a sum is the natural repair. Even so, the procedure pins down exactly which transactions the batch contains. The runtime scheduler should still adapt. If a transaction finishes before its declared ceiling, later work can start sooner and the batch can save time. The executed order must keep the causal order that Definition 13 and the account conflicts imply.

Algorithm 6 sorts with the relation above, charges the inclusion fee on every transaction it considers, and tries to charge the priority fee. If the priority charge fails, the transaction is skipped after the inclusion charge and is not scheduled. Otherwise the routine searches free spaces, each recorded as a start, an end, and a lane, beginning as one full span of length bcu on every lane. It repeatedly takes the minimum remaining space and walks already scheduled work, plus a dummy entry, ordered by end position. A helper decides whether the transaction fits at a candidate position given the accounts that are still busy past that position.

A fit records the position, the compute length, and the accounts, adds the transaction to the result, and splits off any leftover space before and after it. The helper returns the original space unchanged when the remaining length is below the compute limit or the accounts intersect the busy set. After the scan, the result is sorted again and returned. The line that sets the candidate position is not fully readable: after the start time, a large broken symbol stands where the second argument of the maximum should be next to a position-plus-length term.

sections.heading: 3.9 Parameters
paragraphs: Some parameters are implicit and differ in every epoch. The node count n is one of them. The paper states that at the time of writing, n is about 800. That figure stands beside the earlier role sketch, which put the validator count at about 1,000. Table 1 then gives suggested values for the main parameters. It sets 16 proposers and 256 attesters. Because the shred count Gamma_p equals the attester count, 256 pshreds are created and sent. Because the recovery threshold is a quarter of the attester count, 64 pshreds recover a pslice. Because a batch's attestation count is half the attester count, a batch includes 128 attestations. The maximum number of pslices per proposer per cycle is 4. The cycle duration is 50 ms.

The attestation window lambda is defined as the ceiling of the delivery bound divided by the cycle duration, plus one, and the table sets it to 6 cycles. Schedule replacement takes 32 cycles. Data is sent to 2 next leaders. The per-transaction compute limit is 1.4 million compute units. The batch compute limit, which the table calls the makespan, is 2 million compute units. There are 4 parallel execution lanes. The fee payer reserve is 0.001 SOL.
